activities.anchor: Watch it work on a gridworld
activities.caption: which curve is the learned Q-value?
activities.name: rlxGridTrace

config.prompt: Goal worth 10, γ = 0.9. Which curve matches the learned Q-value as the agent's starting cell steps away from the goal?
config.why: 10 → 9 → 8.1 → 7.29 — value propagates backward through the map like heat, each step multiplied by γ; following Q's gradient from any cell walks the agent to the goal.

activities.anchor: RL learns a plan, a fixed sequence of moves
activities.caption: true or false — policy or plan?
activities.name: rlxPolicyJudge

statements.s: RL learns a policy — a mapping from every situation to an action.
statements.why: Which is why a trained agent handles situations its designer never anticipated.

statements.s: RL learns a plan — a fixed sequence of moves.
statements.why: The learned artefact is a policy or value function, not a script; model-based methods plan too, but the learned object is still a policy.

statements.s: AlphaGo's tree search is a hybrid: model-based planning on top of learned networks.
statements.why: The lesson's exact framing — deep policy and value networks with tree search trained on human games and self-play.

statements.s: Deep Q-networks replaced the lookup table with a neural network and a different update rule.
statements.why: Same update, deeper function: DQN (Mnih et al. 2015) swapped the table for a network and learned dozens of Atari games from raw pixels.

activities.anchor: Every RL agent is a gambler
activities.caption: file the methods — three ways to budget exploration
activities.name: rlxBanditBuckets

config.prompt: The multi-armed bandit's toolkit — file each method:

items.label: acts greedily with probability 1 − ε, randomly with probability ε
usually with ε decaying over time — explore early, exploit late
prefers actions whose value estimates are wide
upper-confidence: try things you don't know yet
drives exploration where external rewards are rare

config.why: No fixed strategy is provably optimal in general — so production bandits (ad selection, clinical trials, headline ranking) manage the trade-off explicitly, where exploring on real users costs money.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the exploration budget
activities.name: rlxExploreSpot

config.prompt: This deployment review contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Pure exploitation freezes at the first decent option; pure exploration never banks the winnings.
Epsilon-greedy acts randomly with probability ε, usually decaying over time.
Once training ends, exploration can stop — the policy is finished.
Real environments drift: new products, new adversaries, new users.
Production bandit systems often keep a small permanent ε rather than decaying it to zero.
config.correction: Exploration is maintenance, not a phase — an agent that stops asking whether its value estimates are still true has silently re-entered the exploitation trap.
config.why: Stationary problems can freeze a deployed policy; drifting ones reopen the trade-off forever, which is why the permanent ε exists.

activities.caption: pair each mitigation with its move
activities.name: rlxCreditMatch

config.prompt: Blame is diffused across time — pair each mitigation with what it does:

pairs.right: propagates value estimates backward one step at a time
adds small intermediate signals — injecting the designer's biases, creating new hacking opportunities
compares an action against the policy's average rather than against zero
nudge action probabilities in proportion to how episodes scored — the engine behind RLHF

config.why: Reward variance grows with horizon, so learning signal decays roughly exponentially with the gap between action and reward — the unforgiving statistics of credit assignment.

activities.caption: rebuild the landmark ladder, backgammon to Go
activities.name: rlxLandmarkOrder

config.prompt: One recipe, four breakthroughs — put them in order:
items: TD-Gammon learns backgammon by playing itself, no human games (1992)
AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol — deep networks plus tree search, human games plus self-play (2016)
Move 37: a shoulder hit professional commentary initially scored as a mistake
AlphaGo Zero learns from self-play alone and surpasses its ancestor
AlphaZero generalises the recipe to chess and shogi
config.why: Each landmark shares the precondition that makes RL shine: a fast, faithful simulator that grants unlimited cheap mistakes.

activities.caption: drag the divider — brute force or learned judgement?
activities.name: rlxBruteCompare

config.prompt: Two readings of AlphaGo — drag between them:

before.label: Brute force reading
before.text: The computer simply calculated faster than humans — a deeper search of familiar lines.

after.label: Learned judgement reading
after.text: TD-Gammon reached expert play from pure self-play with no opening book; Move 37 was a different evaluation of the board altogether; AlphaGo Zero surpassed its ancestor with no human games at all.

config.why: What scales is not calculation but the quality of learned judgement guiding the search — a different claim, with different implications for what the method can do outside games.

activities.caption: write the reward — a warehouse robot's objective
activities.name: rlxRewardBranch

config.root: You are specifying the reward for a warehouse robot. Optimisation pressure will find whatever seams you leave.

choices.label: Distance travelled — a proxy for work done
Packages delivered intact and on time
choices.feedback: Closer to the goal — and still a proxy.

choices.label: No reward — imitation of human demonstrators only

spin.text: The boat-race seam: the agent spins in circles hitting respawning boost targets, scoring more than by finishing the race — the objective function working perfectly on a wrong objective.

closer.text: Better aligned, still a proxy — and the problem scales with capability: a stronger optimiser finds subtler seams (the Tetris agent that paused forever was doing exactly what it was told).

imitate.text: No optimisation pressure, no hacking — but also none of RL's signature wins: superhuman play came from pressure on a score, wherever a fast, faithful simulator exists.

config.why: Rewards are proxies for goals we cannot specify; the divergence between specified reward and intended goal is the specification problem — the entry point to AI alignment.
